description: Second precision sample: match rows no audit had read, 100 of Vattel and 50 of Burlamaqui, read by Claude Opus (tools/transcription/PRECISION_PROMPT.md).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian rule in nearly the same words: contracting parties must express themselves so as to be understood by each other.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same mixed favourable/odious case with Grotius's specific example of a change to agreements made for the good of peace.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note names Montesquieu's Esprit des loix as the source of his translation of the Pomponius passage at this point.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's rule restates Wolff's § 386, and the whole sentence follows Wolff § 427, which recalls § 386 in the same oath context.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same a fortiori rule for truces: much less may one solicit the enemy's garrisons or subjects to defect.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 111 gives the same argument and the same common-well example: the one actually using the thing uses his right and cannot be displaced.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel builds § 120 on Wolff § 135 (self-love, then the citizen's undertaking to promote the nation's good), but he turns Wolff's argument for the nation's self-love into the citizen's love of the state.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius (note: III.IX.6), takes up his question on a prisoner's goods in neutral country alienated by the captor, and declares it void on his own principles.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's sentence word for word: distinguish the positive laws carefully from the natural or necessary law of nations without treating them separately.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the stock maxim that no one can bind himself to the illicit is shared; Vattel uses it for restrictive interpretation, while Wolff § 658 uses it on the lawfulness of war alliances, a point Grotius and Pufendorf also make.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared point, that a war on a new cause does not break the peace, is Grotius's, whom Vattel cites here; Vattel's point about old treaties surviving the restoration is not in Wolff § 1025.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-translation of Wolff's proposition that formal war is to be held just on both sides as to its effects.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Clause-by-clause rendering of Wolff's rule on quarter for those laying down arms and life for those capitulating in battle or siege, deduced from the limits of the right to kill.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel opens his rules on neutral trade with Grotius III.1.5's distinction between goods of no use in war (free trade) and goods for war, and his footnote cites that very section.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's specific duty (Inst. § 1108) that a nation must contribute what it can to the preservation and perfection of others is Vattel's first general law.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius and reproduces his Ulysses/Ciconians example almost word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same two-step theorem as Wolff: a protected nation may make treaties unless the protection treaty bars it, but never one contrary to that treaty.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian argument that receiving a fugitive hostage would approve his flight and break faith, but Vattel recasts the sentence and adds returning him.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note names Grotius III.ii.6, the section on whether reprisals may extend to the lives of subjects, for Grotius's advice to abstain.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the Wolffian thesis that a nation seizing unoccupied land acquires empire together with dominion, in parallel words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §3 derives nations' use of natural law from their being persons in a state of nature, while Vattel's §5 argues from men not ceasing to be men in civil union; only the commonplace conclusion is shared, and Wolff §3 matches Vattel §6.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the stock principle that force is lawful only when milder means fail is shared, and Wolff § 782 applies it to the use of force within war, not to settling disputes.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel reports the absolutists' argument that the nation reserved nothing when giving absolute power (Grotius I.3.8's full transfer used against restraining kings) and refutes it with a tacit reservation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-translation of Wolff's proposition that a weak nation may submit on agreed terms, the pact of subjection measuring both parties' rights.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence from Wolff: no new war for the same cause, 'perpetual' peace meaning only that, special versus general transaction, and renunciation barring later proof of title.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian ground (Prolegomena § 5 note, not § 136) that nations are bound by natural law because men forming them remain subject to it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's tacit faith rests on tacit consent and binds like express faith, followed by the rule on what is tacitly agreed, as in Vattel; the passage is in § 560, not § 660.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument: another nation's failure to declare war does not excuse us from declaring, since its fault does not license ours.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same criterion in the same ransom question: the captive counts as free from the moment he is allowed to leave.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note cites Grotius Liv. III ch. 16 for examples of generals returning recaptured booty, which this section gives.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's man/citizen/nation analogy (each must perfect itself so as to be useful to others) is carried over in the same order.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: On the same question of desert lands within a nation's territory Vattel (following Wolff) denies what Grotius II.2.17 allows, and treats Grotius's Ansibarii/Tacitus example the same way; implicit, but a specific correction.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same objection to the doctrine that the nation stays neutral in a succession dispute, with the same 'Quoi!' and tranquil-spectator rhetoric.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That a truce binds subjects only once known is a stock rule (Grotius III.21.5, Wolff); nothing specific links the two sentences beyond it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's duty to coin a sufficient quantity sits beside the intrinsic/extrinsic value rule, as in Wolff's § 803 on money from which this sentence comes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's representative character par excellence, representing the master's person and dignity, is Wolff's special representative character (faculty of bearing the sender's person).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's reason in the same question (sovereign may forbid foreigners to own immovables) translates Wolff §333's premise that no foreigner can claim a right in another's territory.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The restoration rule is common (Grotius III.20.55 n. 1 has it too); Wolff § 543 is about hostages given for hostages and only recalls § 502, and Vattel's next lines reject Wolff's § 503.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Grotius's question on alliances with those of another religion and names Grotius at once.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The wording is close, but in Wolff (a phrase from § 710) it is the adversary who offers equitable terms after a declaration, while Vattel makes it the sovereign's own duty to offer them.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 194 on commercial treaties: take care to commit nothing contrary to the nation's duties to itself and to others, rendered closely.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same voluntary-law argument as Inst. § 1215: each nation judges its own necessity and abuse is hard to determine, so hostile acts count as lawful for both sides and any excess is left to conscience.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's definition word for word (conservatio gentis consistit in duratione consociationis), so the row is a translation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §§ 510-511: the sovereign's power to dispose of subjects grounds the right to give hostages, and the one given must go whether he wills or not; the wording differs.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's definition of a nation's glory (praise of the good and expert, earned by intellectual and moral virtues and their deeds) with the same double source, nation and citizens.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note (a) names Bynkershoek, Juge compétent ch. 16 § 6, which treats the ambassador's immovables and unrelated movables.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the stock maxim that a guarantee saves a third party's right, with nothing more specific shared.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule with the same exception: the acceptor's words govern unless they refer back to the offeror's.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that sovereigns named only to show who made the treaty does not make it personal is the Digest maxim (Pedius/Ulpian) that Vattel himself credits and calls repeated by all authors; nothing points to Wolff § 415 in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.locus: Dialogue I (Charles XII / Pierre le Grand)
rows.reason: Only a stock list of bereaved families (father, son, husband) is shared, used in the dialogue for Charles XII's ruined subjects and in the Droit des gens for the reparation an unjust prince owes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument for ambassadorial immunity: the receiving state would always find fault in an ambassador's conduct and call it a crime.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.locus: Sur le droit de domaine et droit commun
rows.reason: Vattel's own storm-tossed ship and plague-ship example in nearly the same words and structure.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same presumption that riverside land is bounded by the river in case of doubt, with a parallel 'because nothing is more natural/proper' clause.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel translates Wolff's threefold end of war and its offensive/defensive allocation almost word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state Wolff's general/special transaction distinction (Inst. § 764): a special transaction leaves other or later claims to the thing open.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius (note: III.XXIV.1) for what is contained in the nature of certain acts, Grotius's own phrase.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same proposition, structure and exception: a permission granted to all nations cannot be refused to one without particular cause.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Ysendick episode (garrison fires on Maurice's trumpeter, prince's resentment) retold in other words, with Wicquefort cited in the note.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's preface restates Wolff's own preface: duties of individuals applied to nations must be modified according to the nature of their subjects.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared clause is Wolff's stock formula of nations as free persons in the state of nature, which Vattel repeats elsewhere and Formey renders the same way; nothing ties this passage to Formey's section.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's rules on restoring places follow Wolff §§ 1001-1002: return them as taken, no demolition before restitution, wartime razing remitted by the amnesty.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's quiet retreat during a burial truce breaks no promise, as Grotius rules on Philip's retreat (Livy XXXI.38, a burial truce) being nothing contrary to the truce.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel reports and rejects the view that the manner of killing is indifferent, which is Grotius's natural-law claim about sword or poison.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific rule from Wolff § 955: a released prisoner who has not yet paid his ransom and is taken again owes both ransoms.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §140 distinguishes patria from locus nativitatis, which confers no right, the distinction Vattel uses for a child born of a foreigner.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same inference as Wolff § 145: since any right can be removed as punishment, exile can be a punishment.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same praised example of Mucius Scaevola in the same argument separating lawful surprise from assassination; Vattel cites Grotius III.4.18 in the next note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state that a state cannot make treaties contrary to those already binding it, in nearly the same words, so the wording is close rather than loose.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 678 is about a treaty of neutrality and forbids any help at all, while Vattel limits it to what serves directly in war; the list of troops and arms is common to Grotius, Barbeyrac and others.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same two-part rule as Wolff § 924, including the point that an indication that the enemy still claims an unguarded place forbids taking it.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Vattel's text follows Grotius II.16.16.3 on Pedius and Ulpian, and his note gives Barbeyrac's Digest reference word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both give the duty to protect and favour commerce followed by care of roads and safety, then charges to cover costs, from the shared Wolffian sequence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's split between things serving war and things 'd'usage en tout tems' like food, unless destined for war, follows Grotius's classes of goods, but in a different sentence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel opens with Grotius's rule that a treaty made by a republic is real by its nature, in nearly the same words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same justification as Wolff § 1003: names in a peace treaty are taken in the sense the experts of the time gave them, because those who make peace are experts and mean what they then had in mind.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same transition from extension to restriction with the same words ('on resserre aussi ... une promesse ... la signification des termes'), grounded on the reason as in Grotius §§ 22-23.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's second collision rule (permitting law yields to forbidding law) is Grotius's first rule and its corollary in the same sequence of rules.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific point: a well-ordered state provides inns for travellers, recast from Wolff's negative form.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's preface takes Wolff's point that natural-law duties must be adapted to suit nations when applied to them.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Camillus's maxim is given in Barbeyrac's exact French wording from the note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 650's specific remedy against a growing power, confederation of the threatened states for common security, beside the right of arms, is Vattel's gentler means.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes Grotius's rule that aid given to an enemy needs a fresh declaration before war on the helper, and then discusses Grotius's Manlius example.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule and same reasoning: with an alternative of penalty or arms the choice belongs to the injured party.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's truce rule (subjects bound only from notification, not punished for prior acts, sovereigns make reparation) is applied to the peace treaty, Vattel saying it is as with the truce.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius III.20.54: the state that gave the hostage cannot receive and keep her, with the same Cloelia/Porsenna example.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule as Grotius III.21.13: private breaches do not break the truce, but a state that will not punish the offenders is deemed to approve them.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument from Wolff (actually § 210): a nation abusing an exclusive sale to charge an unfair price sins against natural law but does no injury.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Identical Latin quotation with the same De viris illustribus cap. LXXI reference as Grotius's note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff (§ 473-474, not § 586) holds the unratifying sovereign owes only restitution of what enriched it, the doctrine Vattel applies to Caudium.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same qualification that a new cause with some plausible colour does not make taking up arms a breach of the peace, as in Grotius III.XX.28.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel quotes Grotius's example of punishing the cannibal ancient Gauls and rejects his claimed right to punish nations for crimes against nature.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §§ 716-717: declaring war is not meant to let the enemy prepare an unjust defence, so it may be made at the frontier with an army or after entering the territory.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Westphalia courier example with nearly the same words (route marked, passports useless off it).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both rest on the administrator-not-proprietor doctrine and the phrase 'quant à la substance', but the Questions passage is about the people transferring the empire, and Vattel's is about the prince alienating public goods.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of the rights of majesty as all rights without which sovereign power cannot be exercised to the greatest public good.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same interpretive rule (the sense fitting the subject matter is preferred) with the same reasoning and the truce day/night example.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Formey § XVII has the same Wolffian sequence (use of common things, first to lay hands on a thing for use cannot be dispossessed) in near-identical French.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The passage renders Wolff § 341 (a people of men refused wives may take them by force, Roman example), but the Wolff note marks the following sentence that Vattel corrects, so this sentence is paraphrase rather than citation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Grotian argument: whatever is left unassigned in a country occupied as a whole, lakes included, stays with the people who took the territory.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's specific doctrine that the owner nation judges whether a use is innocent and others must defer; Vattel adds that reasons must be given (the passage is in JG § 349, not § 55).

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes Pufendorf's sentence on permission word for word and names him.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui copies Barbeyrac's Devoirs I.i.12 on overcoming inclinations, including the clause 'la gloire qui suit une si belle victoire'.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui says he departs from Grotius's definition of law as too vague, and note (a) cites Grotius I.i.9.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The Élémens keep the same definition of droit as faculty word for word, with the Principes adding 'd'une certaine manière' and the self-regarding use.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both use the promise-keeping example and the answer 'God commands it', but Locke uses it to show that moral rules need proof and get different reasons, while Burlamaqui asks how God's will is known.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.locus: Part I, ch. VI (sanction des loix naturelles)
rows.reason: Burlamaqui makes the same concessive argument in the same chapter on the sanction of natural laws: even if a future state is uncertain or merely possible, a wise man should choose virtue.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the Pufendorfian notion of the accessory state as arising from a human act is shared; Burlamaqui's point that such states are not common to all men is not in this source sentence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's definition of positive law is followed clause by clause, with God's will in place of the legislator's.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Note (a) cites Grotius I.I § 10, the passage distinguishing natural law on things independent of human will from natural law on things following a human act.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui denies Pufendorf's claim that failing one condition of conformity makes an action bad; for him it is only indifferent.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The chapter title states the same thesis in nearly the same words as the Élémens' corresponding chapter: natural law is sufficiently notified.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Identical clause on moral maxims remote from first principles needing a long chain of reasoning, in the same context of probable conscience.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Pufendorf (note: DNG I.VI §§ 6, 8) for the conditions that make man susceptible of obligation, which § 6 begins to set out.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Barbeyrac's note (thumb-cutting Romans, then liability for undertaking what one knew or could easily know exceeds one's strength), clause nearly word for word.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The note names Pufendorf I.1.19, which sets out the kinds of moral power and right (perfect and imperfect, personal and communicable) that the paragraph distinguishes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That natural law is sufficiently notified through reason is common doctrine; Burlamaqui's list of law's conditions has nothing specific to Pufendorf II.3.20.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.locus: Part I, ch. IV (§ on the sovereign and subjects)
rows.reason: Same argument in nearly the same words: reason counsels resisting a malevolent power, and a right to resist excludes the obligation to obey.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Pufendorf's Abrégé, and note (b) cites Devoirs I.ii.3-5, for his account of sovereignty.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same clause 'ce seroit renoncer à son devoir, ce qui n'est jamais permis' in the same renunciation-of-rights argument.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's Seneca quotation follows Barbeyrac's French rendering (pour le dédommager, deux choses, la Raison & la Sociabilité, maître de tout), not the Latin.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Barbeyrac's notes on Grotius I.1.9 (his note a), whose note 3 argues permission must be added to obligation as an effect of law, the view he adopts.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same clause word for word ('cela ne préjudicie en aucune manière au droit des autres, qui n'est'), in the same sequence on pardon and imputation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same refutation of the Scholastics' abstract indifference, ending with the near-identical clause on circumstances of persons, times and places.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's later Élémens restate the same sentence on man's absolute dependence on God for life, reason and their advantages.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The passage is in Burlamaqui's quotation of Barbeyrac's argument (note to Grotius / Jugement), which only echoes Pufendorf's self-release argument in other words.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The footnote names Pufendorf I.4.9, the section on mixed actions done under threat of a great evil, which the paragraph follows (some phrases word for word).

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The PDP repeats the PDN definition of civil society word for word.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Note (a) cites Pufendorf DNG I.I § 19, where the four kinds of power that Burlamaqui lists are set out.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same two essential parts of law (disposition, sanction with penalty) and the sanction as the law's force, in the same sentence structure.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes Barbeyrac's note (force only enables the superior to enforce his right) and says the thought is not right.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The sentence on Ulpian's distinction (droit des gens fits man as man, as against man as animal) is copied word for word from Barbeyrac's note.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Barbeyrac's report of Grotius's universal voluntary divine law nearly word for word and agrees with Barbeyrac, so he does not reject this source.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's note reproduces the same Cicero pairing (De Off. II.3 and III.3 on Socrates) as Barbeyrac's note, and cites Pufendorf II.3.10.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.locus: III. Partie, chap. IX, regle 5 (consentement, contrainte)
rows.reason: The Principes and the Élémens share the clause 'défendant formellement toute violence' in the same argument that a forced promise is void.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The sentence on mistaken belief about indifferent things is the same as Barbeyrac's note, word for word.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The objection quotes Barbeyrac's note almost word for word, including the debtor-creditor comparison and the Seneca reference.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence sequence and many words: law said to be naturally known, but not born with us or imprinted from the first moment of existence.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes and then restates Barbeyrac's definition of law with the same words 'impose la nécessité d'agir ou de ne pas agir d'une certaine maniére'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The division of conscience into judgment before and after the action is the stock scholastic antecedent/consequent distinction; the wording parallels Pufendorf but nothing specific shows dependence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Pufendorf on habits: they can be shed if one wills it, they were in our power not to contract, so imputation is not lessened and good habits make actions more praiseworthy.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-identical wording of the view that man is perfect only so far as his way of thinking and acting leads him to his end, happiness; Burlamaqui cites Pouilly ch. VIII.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Natural independence until subjection by convention is a stock definition; the Pufendorf sentence shares the idea but nothing ties Burlamaqui's wording to it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Barbeyrac's note step by step (algebra example, then two men destined to an office), changing the professions.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: PDP I.1.14 has the same sentence: one rule of justice, princes' crime no less, their bad actions having worse consequences than private persons'.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same definition of obligation, but 'restriction' replaces 'resserrement, une limitation', so only the phrase 'de la liberté naturelle produite par la raison' is identical.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of probable conscience, with Pufendorf-Barbeyrac's wording: convinced of the truth of its judgment but unable to demonstrate it, resting on likelihood.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Reworks Barbeyrac's note almost clause by clause: the eternity of natural law was said in contrast to changing civil laws, older than Minos and Solon, as old as mankind.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The clause 'jointes ou non, elles produisent le même effet & suivent les mêmes règles' is taken from Barbeyrac's note on ignorance and error, with the two members swapped.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Pufendorf only reports the voluntarist view in order to answer it, and Burlamaqui follows his answer (God was free to create man or not, but having done so...), so the two agree rather than disagree.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-verbatim reuse of Barbeyrac's dilemma that binding only those who know the laws destroys their universality.
